question.text: Satpura Market-Neutral Fund runs a long-value/short-growth pair book. The team wants to benchmark the long leg separately. Which ratios are typically used to classify a stock as a VALUE stock for style-index purposes (per Section 8.5.3)?

answer.text: High P/B, high P/E, low dividend yield
Low P/B, low P/E, high dividend yield
High P/B, low P/E, high dividend yield
Low P/B, high P/E, low dividend yield

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Per Section 8.5.3: 'Stocks with low P/B, low P/E ratio and high dividend yield are categorized as value stocks. Stocks with high P/B, high P/E ratios and low dividend yield are categorized as growth stocks.' Style indices use these cuts; they have high turnover because valuation ratios migrate constantly. **The Trap:** Option A is the growth-stock profile — exactly inverted. Options C and D are internally inconsistent mixes. **Cross-Exam Context:** XV (RA) and XXI-B (PM) test value-vs-growth classification. XIX-C / XIX-D cover style-index use for AIF benchmarking. Note: S&P and MSCI use slightly different cut-offs — P/B, P/E and forward earnings growth — but the concept is identical. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** For a Cat III long-value/short-growth pair, remember style-index turnover is high — stocks migrate between value and growth camps on every reconstitution date. Build your pair around structural business differences (e.g., FMCG vs new-tech), not just current P/E — otherwise your pair dissolves on the next style-index reshuffle.
